vignette:
She is fifty-four, European, married, and has spent most of her adult life in kitchens. Before the assault, she thinks of herself as someone who could handle heat, noise, pressure, and the rough edges of other people. She has worked as a chef for decades, rising before dawn to inspect deliveries, breaking down fish, barking times across the line, and moving through cramped spaces with the instinctive economy of someone who knows exactly where every knife, pan, and body is likely to be. She takes pride in being steady. Her husband has always teased that nothing rattles her.

The assault happens after a late shift nearly two years ago. She stays behind to finish inventory and lock up. The restaurant is quiet in a way she usually enjoys, the hoods still ticking as they cool, the smell of garlic and bleach hanging in the air. As she carries a crate toward the back exit, a man forces his way in through the service entrance. At first she thinks he wants money. She tries to give him access to the office, telling him to take whatever he wants. Instead he corners her in the narrow passage by the walk-in refrigerator and attacks her. Later, when she tries to describe it, what comes back first is not a sequence but fragments: the cold metal door against her shoulder blades, the damp floor under one knee, his breath sour with alcohol, the sound of a ladle clattering somewhere far away. She remembers thinking, with surreal clarity, that the stock on the stove would burn.

In the immediate aftermath, she does what she has always done under pressure: she moves. She calls emergency services. She answers questions. She phones her husband in a voice that sounds to her like someone else’s. In the days that follow, people praise her for being composed. She returns to the restaurant sooner than her husband expects, telling everyone she needs routine. She ties on her apron, writes specials on the board, tastes a sauce, and almost convinces herself she is back.

Then the kitchen begins to change around her. The service entrance becomes unbearable. If someone comes in unexpectedly from behind, her whole body jerks before she can stop it. The slam of the walk-in door sends a jolt through her chest. At night she wakes drenched in sweat, certain for a few seconds that he is in the room. Sometimes she dreams she is pinned against the refrigerator again, unable to breathe, and wakes kicking at the sheets while her husband reaches for her. She hates the look on his face when she flinches from his touch before she recognizes him.

She starts checking locks repeatedly at home and at work, circling back three or four times even after she knows she has secured the doors. She positions younger staff near the front and avoids being alone in the building. If a supplier arrives early, she feels panic rising before she can identify why. She finds herself studying men’s hands, shoulders, and exits. During service, when the tickets pile up, she can still perform for stretches on muscle memory, but her concentration frays. She loses track of orders she has read twice. Once, when a prep cook drops a tray behind her, she crouches instinctively, hands over her head, while the whole line goes silent.

At home she becomes smaller and harder to reach. Her husband asks if she wants to go out to dinner, and she says no because crowded rooms make her skin prickle. Friends stop inviting them after enough refusals. She sits in the living room with the television on but cannot follow the plot because her mind keeps snagging on the assault, replaying it without warning while she folds laundry or chops onions. She tells herself not to think about it, and then feels ambushed by it anyway. Some mornings the smell of bleach in her own kitchen sends her back so abruptly that she has to grip the counter until the room steadies.

What troubles her almost as much as the fear is the change in who she feels herself to be. She has always been direct, funny, sometimes sharp-tongued in the way chefs often are, but fundamentally open with her team. Now she is irritable and suspicious. She snaps at mistakes she once would have corrected calmly. She no longer lingers after service for a drink with staff. She watches everyone leave, then scans each room before locking up, heart pounding. Her world has narrowed to routes she considers safe, tasks she can control, and a constant effort to keep herself from coming apart.

When she speaks about the assault now, she often does so with her jaw set and her hands clasped tightly in her lap, as if bracing against impact. She says she knows, logically, that the man is gone and that she survived. But her body does not seem to know it. In her body, the danger is still present: in the hiss of a burner, in footsteps at her back, in the lonely quiet of a kitchen after closing. She misses the version of herself who could stay until the last light was off and the last door locked without feeling hunted.
